Learning Objectives
Review the diagnosis, presentation, and management of common inflammatory rheumatic
diseases.
Assess the high use of arthroplasty among patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases,
such as rheumatoid arthritis, despite the widespread use of potent disease-modifying
antirheumatic drugs and targeted therapies, including biologics.
Identify the manifestations of rheumatic diseases that contribute to an increased risk of
postoperative adverse events.
Determine the approach for balancing the risks of infection and delayed wound healing if
glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive medications are continued compared with the
potential for disease flare-up if withheld.
Apply current recommendations for management of immunosuppressive medications in
patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases at the time of total hip arthroplasty and total

Arthroplasty in Patients With Inflammatory Rheumatic Diseases
Patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases have an increased risk of requiring large joint
arthroplasty despite the increased use of biologics and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs
(DMARDs).

Arthroplasty in Patients With Inflammatory Rheumatic Diseases
Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis, or
spondylarthritis (SpA) typically present with joint problems; therefore, orthopaedists
must be familiar with the diagnosis and management of these diseases. In addition,
patients with rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, or SpA continue to undergo and benefit from
arthroplasty; rates of large joint replacement in patients with rheumatoid arthritis have
not changed over decades despite the widespread use of potent DMARDs and biologics,
and the rates of arthroplasty have increased in patients with SpA and SLE.1,2 SpA
encompasses patients with ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis (PsA), reactive
arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease–associated arthritis. Patients with rheumatoid
arthritis have double the lifetime risk of undergoing total hip arthroplasty (THA)/total
knee arthroplasty compared with the general population. These systemic inflammatory
diseases are associated with extra-articular manifestations that are linked to surgical
complications, and the medications used to manage these diseases may suppress the
immune system, increasing the risk for infection.3 In 2016, 50% of patients with
rheumatoid arthritis who underwent arthroplasty were being treated with biologics or
other targeted DMARDs, 80% were being treated with methotrexate or other
conventional synthetic DMARDs, and 30% were being treated with
glucocorticoids.4 Orthopaedists should be familiar with rheumatic diseases and their
management.
Rheumatoid Arthritis
Pathology of Disease

9/3/26, 7:25 AM

2/19


Pathology of Disease
Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease caused by a cell-
mediated immune response against soft tissues, cartilage, and bone. The disease is
characterized by synovial inflammation and hyperplasia, autoantibody production,
cartilage and bone erosion, and destruction and systemic involvement.5 Common
markers of rheumatoid arthritis that aid in diagnosis include anti-citrullinated protein
antibody and rheumatoid factor. Rheumatoid factor is an immunoglobulin M antibody
that acts against native immunoglobulin G antibodies. The etiology of rheumatoid
arthritis remains unclear, with theories related to genetics and infection proposed.
Diagnosis is based on patient history, physical examination, imaging studies, and
laboratory markers.
Patient Presentation

Patient Presentation
Patients often present with multiple symmetric joint involvement, and rheumatoid
arthritis can affect the hands, feet, knees, hips, cervical spine, elbows, ankles, and
shoulders. Common findings on physical examination of patients with severe
rheumatoid arthritis include subcutaneous nodules, joint swelling, sparing of the distal
interphalangeal joints of the fingers, and ulnar deviation of the metacarpophalangeal
joints. Diagnostic imaging studies may reveal periarticular erosions, osteopenia,
concentric joint space narrowing, and protrusio acetabuli (Figure 1).

Figure 1 AP hand radiographs demonstrate the progression of erosions from the time
the initial radiograph was obtained (A) to the time the follow-up radiograph was
obtained 6 years later (B). Severe narrowing of the radiocarpal and midcarpal joints and
the right second and third and the left second and third metacarpophalangeal joints is
observed, indicating marginal erosive changes. (Courtesy of Susan M. Goodman, MD,
New York, NY.)
Management

Management
The management of rheumatoid arthritis primarily is medical, with the first line of
management consisting of the use of NSAIDs and corticosteroids to control symptoms
and the early use of DMARDs, including traditional synthetic drugs, such as
methotrexate, and biologic-targeted therapies to prevent or decrease joint damage.
DMARDs and biologics have resulted in the decreased use of high-dose glucocorticoids
for the management of rheumatoid arthritis. Joint inflammatory arthritis is managed

4/19

similar to osteoarthritis via physical therapy; corticosteroid injections; and surgical
management, including total joint arthroplasty.
Postoperative Adverse Events

Postoperative Adverse Events
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis have an increased risk for periprosthetic joint
infection that persists over the lifetime of the implant, dissimilar from patients with
osteoarthritis, for whom the risk abates after 1 to 2 years postopertively.6 Patients with
rheumatoid arthritis have an increased risk for allogeneic blood transfusion, which may
contribute to the infection risk and does not appear to be mitigated by the use of
tranexamic acid.7 Infection also is associated with active rheumatoid arthritis, and only
30% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis have low disease activity or are in remission at
the time of arthroplasty. Staphylococcus aureus is more likely to colonize patients with
rheumatoid arthritis who are being treated with the use of biologics (37%) compared
with patients being treated with conventional synthetic DMARDs (24%) and compared
with patients with osteoarthritis (20%).8
Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
Pathology of Disease

Pathology of Disease
SLE is a chronic autoimmune disorder that more commonly affects young women,
consisting of immune complex deposition in the joints, skin, kidneys, lungs, heart, blood
vessels, and nervous system. The underlying pathophysiology remains unclear, and
diagnosis is based on symptoms, physical examination findings, and laboratory analysis.

Patient Presentation

Patient Presentation
Joint involvement is common, with pain and swelling of multiple joints, including the
hands, wrists, and hips. Diagnosis is based on criteria, including a malar rash, joint
swelling, and synovitis, as well as laboratory findings of antinuclear antibodies and anti-
double stranded DNA.
Management

Management
Management primarily is medical via NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, antimalarial agents,
DMARDs, and biologics. Osteonecrosis of the femoral head is more common in patients
with SLE than in patients with rheumatoid arthritis given high-dose glucocorticoid
therapy and often leads to end-stage secondary osteoarthritis requiring total hip
replacement (Figures 2 and 3).

Postoperative Adverse Events

Postoperative Adverse Events
For patients with SLE, the risk of adverse events reflects the systemic nature of the
disease and the medications, and more than 70% of patients undergoing THA/total knee
arthroplasty are being treated with immunosuppressant medications at the time of
arthroplasty.9 Adverse events are increased in patients with a recent SLE-related
hospitalization. Risks of postoperative acute renal failure, venous thromboembolism,
pneumonia, septicemia, and death are highest in patients hospitalized for SLE within 6
months of surgical treatment.10 Additional risks in patients with SLE are hip dislocation
and falls that result in fracture.11
Seronegative Spondyloarthropathies

Pathology of Disease

Pathology of Disease
Spondylarthritis includes patients with ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive
arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease–associated arthritis. Ankylosing spondylitis is
more commonly diagnosed in Caucasian males, and classically involves the spine, with
bridging spinal osteophyte formation, sacroiliitis, uveitis, and enthesis (Figure 4).

Figure 4 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of a spine demonstrate interbody and
posterior lateral fusion of the lumbar spine and ankylosis at the sacroiliac joints,
characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis. (Courtesy of Susan M. Goodman, MD, New York,
NY.)
Patient Presentation

Patient Presentation
SEND FEEDBACK

10/19

Diagnosis is based on the presence of inflammatory back pain and imaging studies
revealing sacroiliitis. Diagnosis is supported by the presence of human leukocyte antigen
B27. Patients with psoriatic arthritis often presents with hand involvement, with distal
interphalangeal arthritis, nail pitting, uveitis, and a rash with silvery plaques over the
extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees.
Management

Management
Management primarily is nonsurgical via NSAIDs; physical therapy; and targeted biologic
therapies, including tumor necrosis factor inhibitors or interleukin-17 blockers. Surgical
management of the spine includes fusion or corrective osteotomy, and large joints are
managed via total joint arthroplasty. Patients with psoriatic arthritis are treated
medically via NSAIDs, corticosteroids, DMARDs and biologics. Patients with ankylosing
spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis are more prone to heterotopic ossification after total
joint arthroplasty; therefore, NSAIDs or radiation therapy prophylaxis should be
considered.
Postoperative Adverse Events

Postoperative Adverse Events
Patients with ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis are at risk for heterotopic
ossification after arthroplasty, and anterior hip dislocation is reported in patients with
lumbar spine fusion. A single treatment with low-dose radiation therapy or with NSAIDs
(such as indomethacin) can be used as prophylaxis against heterotopic ossification.
Patients with ankylosing spondylitis also are at risk for pulmonary complications because
of chest wall motion restriction caused by thoracic spine fusion and inflammation of the
chest wall. Because patients with advanced disease may have severe chest wall
restriction limiting thoracic volume expansion, they use their diaphragm to breathe;

therefore, scalene blocks are relatively contraindicated in these patients given the
frequency of ipsilateral (transient) diaphragm paralysis. Systemic complications,
including venous thromboembolism, and infection may be increased in patients with
SpA; however, the literature is conflicting and may reflect the difficulty of case
ascertainment in administrative data sets.12-14
Anesthesia Considerations
Evaluate the cervical spine in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis.
Consider fiberoptic intubation in patients with cervical spine involvement.

Anesthesia Considerations
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis may have cervical spine
involvement. In patients with rheumatoid arthritis, cervical spine instability, either
atlantoaxial or subaxial, with subluxation may compress the spinal cord in severe
situations; therefore, manipulation of the neck for intubation may produce spinal cord
injury. Patients at highest risk are those with long-standing erosive rheumatoid arthritis,
a group with which considerable overlap exists with those undergoing arthroplasty.
Because one-third of patients with cervical spine involvement are asymptomatic,
screening patients in the high-risk group via lateral cervical spine flexion/extension
radiographs can detect those at risk.15,16 Consultation with an experienced
anesthesiologist and consideration of fiberoptic intubation are important in these
patients. For patients with ankylosing spondylitis, the fused cervical spine becomes rigid,
and because of paradoxical vertebral osteoporosis, a risk for fracture is present during
intubation and surgical positioning.
Perioperative Management of Antirheumatic Therapy
Wean glucocorticoids preoperatively; continue the usual daily dose in the perioperative period
rather than the use of stress-dose steroids.

Withhold biologics preoperatively based on the dosing interval and postoperatively until the
wound has healed (typically 14 days).
Continue conventional DMARDs in the perioperative period.

Perioperative Management of Antirheumatic Therapy
Modifiable risk factors for postoperative infections include smoking and medication
management, given the well-documented association between DMARDs and biologics
and increased infection. Perioperative management of immunosuppressive medications
has been addressed in a collaborative effort between the American Association of Hip
and Knee Surgeons and the American College of Rheumatology, which was based on a
consensus approach informed by a thorough literature review17 (Table 1).
Conventional synthetic DMARDs, such as methotrexate, leflunomide,
hydroxychloroquine, or sulfasalazine, appear safe to continue in the perioperative
period and have not been linked to postoperative infections. Biologic DMARDs increase
the risk of infection in nonsurgical settings; therefore, surgical management should be
performed at the end of the dosing cycle. For example, if a biologic is administered every
2 weeks, surgical management is performed during week three. For patients with severe
SLE, the panel recommended that any decision be made in consultation with a patient’s
rheumatologist because the risk for flare-up in patients with severe disease may pose a
greater risk than continuing the medication through surgical management.
Medications can be restarted after the wound has healed, typically 10 to 14 days
postoperatively, if no indication of a surgical site infection or infection exists. Careful
assessment of wound healing is advised before restarting biologics
Glucocorticoids increase the risk for infection and impair wound healing, effects that are
linked to dose and duration of therapy. The practice of administering supraphysiologic
doses of glucocorticoids, or stress dose steroids, developed for long-term steroid use,
blunts the innate ability of the adrenal gland to secrete elevated levels during periods of
physiologic stress, such as during surgical management. Early case reports warned of
refractory hypotension if stress dose steroids were not prescribed. A review of this

literature has not supported this practice, and the American College of Rheumatology
and the American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons recommend that the usual daily
dose of glucocorticoid be administered on the day of THA or total knee arthroplasty, with
the dose be tapered, if possible, to 20 mg of prednisone (or equivalent).17 A recent
retrospective review on perioperative glucocorticoid use did not report hypotension in
patients who were not prescribed stress dose steroids; however, an association between
hyperglycemia and catheter-associated urinary tract infections was observed in those
who receive stress dose steroids.18

Summary

Summary
Patients with SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, and SpA frequently present to orthopaedists with
joint problems or as referrals for surgical treatment. Orthopaedists should understand
